subs.text: It's 8:52. You're late.
Six days into your first real job, Leo — and you're already late.
Project manager. At least, that's what the badge says.
The elevator doors are closing. You run.
You make it. Perfect.
Except — you're not alone.
Standing right next to you is Diane Ward. She runs the whole company.
Eleven floors. About thirty seconds. Nobody is speaking.
The doors close. Thirty seconds.
What do you say?
Morning! Big day for the team, huh?
It is. And you must be the new one.
That's warm, and it's natural.
"Huh?" does the real work. It hands her the turn, and a greeting becomes a conversation.
It's casual for a CEO you've never met. Small bet. This time, it pays off.
Good morning, Ms. Ward. It's a pleasure to finally meet you.
Diane, please. Ms. Ward is my mother.
Safe, polite, correct. Nothing here can go wrong.
But listen to the word "finally" — it quietly says you've been hoping for this.
You just spent five seconds creating distance you now have to close.
Good morning.
Good morning.
Two words. Nothing wrong with them.
And nothing memorable either. In a thirty-second window, that spends your turn without buying anything.
She nods. The silence comes back. Now it's heavier.
Floor six. Seven.
Then she does something she doesn't have to do.
So — what are you working on?
Four words. This is the door.
You have maybe twenty seconds before floor eleven.
She asked. Twenty seconds.
What do you do with them?
I'm building a tool that uses AI to cut our campaign copy from three days to three hours.
Three hours. Say that again in the meeting on Thursday.
That's a whole pitch in one breath.
Notice the shape: what it does, then the number. She'll remember three days to three hours long after she forgets your name.
Bold works when the number is real. If it isn't, this is the sentence that ends you.
Can I ask you something first — what slows your marketing team down the most?
Huh. Nobody's asked me that in a while.
You just gave away your twenty seconds to buy better information.
Can I ask you something first — that asks permission before spending her attention. Senior people notice it.
She may not answer today. But she will remember that you asked instead of pushed.
Honestly? I'm still learning where the coffee machine is.
Second floor, past the printers. The good one.
You didn't pitch. You made her laugh at 8:52 in the morning.
That is not nothing. Deals don't close in elevators.
People just decide whether they want the next conversation. She does.
Floor nine. Ten.
Whatever you just said, it landed. She's looking at you now.
The doors are about to open. This is the last thing she'll remember.
Floor eleven. The doors open.
Last words?
Could I get fifteen minutes with you next week?
Fifteen. Tuesday. Email my assistant.
Direct, and specific.
Fifteen minutes is small enough to say yes to. A meeting is not.
Always name the size of the ask. Vague asks get vague answers.
I'll send you one page. If it's boring, you'll never hear from me again.
One page. I'll read it. And I'll tell you if it's boring.
This is confidence with an escape hatch.
You promised one page, and you gave her permission to ignore it.
Low pressure, high memory. Busy people love a small, cancellable ask.
Thanks for the chat, Diane. Have a good one.
You too, Leo. My door's not as far as it looks.
Clean, warm, no ask at all.
Sometimes that's exactly right. You're one week in; you don't have to close anything.
But nothing is scheduled. A warm door still needs someone to knock.
The doors close behind her.
You're alone in a hallway on the eleventh floor.
Whatever happens next — it started in those thirty seconds.
Same elevator. Same thirty seconds. Three different versions of you.
None of them were wrong. They just cost different things.
That's the whole game — knowing what each one costs.
Here's today's challenge.
Find one small window today. A hallway. A coffee line. A call before it starts.
Say the one you didn't pick.
See you tomorrow.
